title: Treasury Bills vs. High-Yield Savings: Which Is Better in the U.S. Today?
description: A comparison of risk-free assets, focusing on yield curves, state tax exemptions, and liquidity.
content:
For safety-conscious investors, the debate in 2025 is between the High-Yield Savings Account (HYSA) and US Treasury Bills (T-Bills). Both are considered 'risk-free'—HYSAs are FDIC insured, and T-Bills are backed by the US Government. However, there are hidden differences. T-Bills often pay slightly higher rates and offer a massive tax advantage for residents of high-tax states. HYSAs offer ultimate liquidity. This guide breaks down the math to help you decide where to park your cash.

Key Takeaways

  • State Tax Exemption: Interest earned on T-Bills is exempt from State and Local income taxes. HYSA interest is fully taxable.
  • Yield Locking: T-Bills lock in a rate for the term (e.g., 6 months). HYSA rates are variable and can drop tomorrow if the Fed cuts rates.
  • Liquidity: HYSAs are liquid instantly. T-Bills must be sold on the secondary market to access cash early (which is easy, but adds a step).
  • The Spread: Historically, T-Bills yield 0.20% - 0.50% more than the best HYSAs.

Why It Matters (US Context)

If you live in California (13.3% top tax rate), New York (10.9%), or Hawaii (11%), T-Bills are the clear winner. The 'Tax-Equivalent Yield' of a 5% T-Bill for a Californian is roughly equal to a 5.7% HYSA—a rate that doesn't exist. Understanding your marginal state tax bracket is key to this decision.

The Math: Tax-Equivalent Yield

Let's assume you have $50,000 in savings and live in New York City with a combined state/city tax rate of 10%.

Scenario A: HYSA at 4.5%

  • Interest Earned: $2,250
  • Federal Tax (24%): -$540
  • State/City Tax (10%): -$225
  • Net After-Tax: $1,485

Scenario B: T-Bills at 4.6%

  • Interest Earned: $2,300
  • Federal Tax (24%): -$552
  • State/City Tax (0%): $0 (Exempt)
  • Net After-Tax: $1,748

Winner: T-Bills put an extra $263 in your pocket simply because of the tax shield. The higher your tax bracket and state taxes, the better T-Bills look.

When to Use Which Account

  1. Use HYSA For: Your immediate checking buffer and Tier 1 Emergency Fund (1 month of expenses). You need this money to be available via ATM or instant transfer.
  2. Use T-Bills For: Your deep savings (House down payment, Tier 2 Emergency Fund). Money you won't touch for at least 4 weeks.
  3. How to Buy T-Bills: Do not use TreasuryDirect.gov (it is clunky). Use a brokerage like Fidelity or Schwab. Go to 'Fixed Income' -> 'New Issues' -> 'Treasury'.
  4. The Ladder Strategy: Buy a 4-week T-Bill every week for 4 weeks. Now, you have one maturing every single week, giving you weekly liquidity with higher yields.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I lose money in T-Bills?

Only if the US Government defaults (highly unlikely) OR if you sell them *early* on the secondary market when rates have risen. If you hold to maturity, you are guaranteed your principal + interest.

Is there a minimum for T-Bills?

Usually $1,000 per bill at brokerages. TreasuryDirect allows $100 minimums.

Do T-Bills compound?

No. They are sold at a discount. You pay $990 and get back $1,000. You must manually reinvest (roll over) the proceeds to get the compounding effect. Most brokers have an 'Auto-Roll' feature.
